=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)
will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.
Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing
bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds
flow.)
Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio
matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.
Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter
and is not expected to be material.
Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course
operating costs.
Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime
above.
Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.
Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and
records are fictional.
1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the
indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including
DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.
2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause
11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final
written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.
3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security
is included.
4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of
every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of
non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.
5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject
to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft
Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or
on-costs apply.
6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external
email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity
timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised
person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation
remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no
loss amount.
7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as
a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.
8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each
(AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether
each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.
9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale
consent is required merely because shares are sold.
10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of
the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the
Buyer has completed its own verification.
11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer
must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer assessment

**The Seller’s package should not be accepted as drafted.** It combines unresolved completion risks with provisions that could prevent recovery for those same risks: broad disclosure, constructive buyer knowledge, and limitations applying to “all Claims”.

The principal concerns are Bluefen’s consent, Riverlark’s debt and security, Ironquay’s IP ownership, omitted completion bonuses, and the unresolved export incident.

This review is based on the supplied summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. Those documents must be checked before settling drafting.

## 1. Completion and price protection

### Bluefen: consent is not yet established

**Evidence:** Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6 million of FY26 revenue, or 30%. No final consent or evidence satisfying its associated conditions is supplied.

**Why push back:** Losing or impairing this relationship could materially change the business being purchased. Reasonable endeavours is only an obligation to try; it does not secure the outcome. Delivery of written consent alone may not satisfy conditions under clause 11.3.

**Buyer position:**
- Make effective Bluefen consent, including satisfaction of applicable conditions, a condition precedent waivable only by the Buyer.
- Require evidence that consent covers this transaction and does not introduce unacceptable fees, termination rights or adverse commercial changes.
- No deemed satisfaction merely on delivery of a consent document.
- Include a longstop date and Buyer termination right if the condition is not satisfied.

### Riverlark: no post-completion release gap

**Evidence:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding; neither repayment nor final security discharge is evidenced.

**Why push back:** The Buyer is acquiring on a debt-free/cash-free basis. A promise to release security after Completion leaves the acquired company exposed and the Buyer dependent on later performance.

**Buyer position:**
- Obtain a current payoff statement, including interest, fees and all secured obligations.
- Arrange repayment directly through the completion funds flow, with the corresponding deduction from Seller proceeds under the agreed price mechanics.
- Require an effective release of security, guarantees and other relevant obligations at Completion. Where registration removal follows administratively, require binding lender release undertakings and controlled discharge arrangements—not an unsecured Seller promise.
- Reconcile the debt adjustment and lender payment so the amount is neither omitted nor deducted twice.

### Completion bonuses: allocate the full cost expressly

**Evidence:** AUD 420,000 is conditionally payable on Completion and continued employment, but is absent from the funds flow. On-costs are unspecified.

**Why push back:** Calling this “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the acquired company from bearing the cost. The agreed AUD 24 million economics could therefore be eroded.

**Buyer position:**
- Review the bonus terms, payment dates and employing entity.
- Require Seller funding or a specific price deduction for the agreed Seller-borne amounts, including applicable employer superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.
- Show payment/funding expressly in the completion statement and funds flow.
- Separate any genuinely post-completion retention component requiring Buyer agreement.
- Avoid double counting amounts already captured in debt, working capital or transaction-expense adjustments.

### Sandbar renewals: investigate before classifying

**Evidence:** Three related renewals total AUD 330,000. Their unavoidable nature, termination rights, accrual status and ordinary-course character are not established.

**Why push back:** The Seller’s “ordinary-course” label is unsupported. Equally, the full AUD 330,000 is **not automatically a debt-like deduction** merely because it is disclosed.

**Buyer position:** Review DD-008 and DD-011 together for commitment dates, service periods, cancellation rights and commercial purpose. Then determine whether amounts belong in working capital, debt-like items, transaction expenses or future operating costs. Restrict new or materially changed commitments before Completion without Buyer consent.

## 2. Known liabilities and ownership risks

### Ironquay: payment-only protection is too narrow

**Evidence:** Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open, but non-payment is not independently verified; no receipt or confirmatory assignment is supplied.

**Why push back:** The risk is not simply a AUD 180,000 invoice. It is whether Paperbark owns the relevant IP and can continue using and commercialising it without challenge.

**Buyer position:**
- Verify all relevant fees and payment status.
- Require cleared payment and effective written confirmation of IP transfer before Completion, preferably through a confirmatory assignment and release.
- Check the scope of Project Materials, background-IP licences and the chain of title from relevant creators.
- Broaden the specific indemnity beyond the invoice to losses from the identified ownership defect or dispute, including reasonable defence and remediation costs.
- Exclude this indemnity from general warranty baskets, disclosure and knowledge defences, with separately negotiated limits and survival.

Payment evidence alone should not substitute for checking that the contractual transfer actually works.

### Export/privacy incident: neither dismiss nor overstate it

**Evidence:** A download link was sent to an unintended external address; approximately 1,240 records may be involved. Access, exact scope and notification requirements remain unresolved.

**Why push back:** There is insufficient evidence to call this a confirmed notifiable breach—but equally no basis to dismiss it as immaterial. Names and business emails can be personal information, and contractual obligations may apply independently of statutory notification requirements.

**Buyer position:**
- Require prompt investigation, containment and preservation of evidence, including access logs, link revocation and recipient follow-up.
- Establish the data involved, access or onward disclosure, applicable privacy obligations and customer notification requirements.
- Obtain updated findings before signing and Completion, together with appropriate interim conduct and cooperation obligations.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the identified pre-completion incident and related failings, covering reasonable investigation, remediation, notification and third-party claim costs; address penalties only to the extent legally recoverable.
- If material uncertainty remains, consider retention/escrow, a completion condition or a price adjustment proportionate to the evidence.

### Title: the register is evidence, not complete protection

**Evidence:** DD-012 records the Seller as holder of all issued shares.

**Why push back:** That does not alone establish unencumbered beneficial ownership, absence of competing rights, or a complete and valid capital structure.

**Buyer position:** Verify the register against issue and transfer records, constitutional documents, relevant searches, certificates and any options, convertibles, trusts or shareholder arrangements. Require full title, capacity and capitalisation warranties, effective transfer deliverables and release of share encumbrances.

## 3. Liability regime: restore meaningful recourse

| Seller position | Buyer concern and recommended response |
|---|---|
| **20% general warranty cap: AUD 4.8m** | Assess against diligence findings, available security and any W&I insurance. Seek a higher general cap; do not extend it automatically to title, tax or specific indemnities. The appropriate percentage is a negotiation point, not established by these documents. |
| **AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 excess-only basket** | The Seller retains the first AUD 250,000 of qualifying losses. Seek lower thresholds and a tipping basket, under which qualifying losses become recoverable once the basket is exceeded. Aggregate related claims to prevent fragmentation. |
| **18-month general warranty period** | Seek a longer period sufficient to identify issues through post-completion reporting and audit cycles. Tax, fundamental warranties and specific indemnities need separate periods. |
| **Title and capacity subject to general limits** | Reject. Seek a separate cap of at least the purchase price, no de minimis/basket, and materially longer survival consistent with the applicable legal framework. |
| **Tax and IP treated as settled under the general regime** | Reopen. Require appropriate substantive warranties. Tax needs a dedicated pre-completion tax covenant/indemnity and survival aligned with relevant assessment periods plus a buffer. IP protection must address ownership, licences and infringement; Ironquay requires separate treatment. |
| **Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to “all Claims”** | Reject the blanket approach. Preserve agreed remedies for price adjustments, debt repayment, covenants, specific indemnities, title, fraud and deliberate concealment, and appropriate equitable relief. Do not allow warranty machinery to neutralise separate payment obligations. |

Review the actual clauses together: a nominal carve-out in clause 12 may be defeated by the definitions or clauses 9.3, 13 or 20.5.

Also:
- Preserve claims notified in time until resolved; review any separate deadline for commencing proceedings.
- Require reasonably available notice particulars, not an excessively technical forfeiture mechanism.
- Ensure contractual limitations do not purport to exclude non-excludable statutory rights. Under Australian law, non-reliance wording can affect the evidence and merits of a misleading-conduct claim, but does not simply eliminate statutory exposure.
- Consider escrow, retention or other security for meaningful recovery, particularly for known risks.

## 4. Disclosure and buyer knowledge: reject blanket risk transfer

### General disclosure

Disclosure of the entire data room, public records and everything “referred to” is too broad. It may leave the Buyer bearing risks that were buried, ambiguous or incompletely investigated.

Seek:
- A **fair-disclosure standard** requiring sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter.
- Specific references to affected warranties and documents.
- A frozen, indexed and retained data-room record.
- No automatic disclosure of documents merely referenced but not supplied.
- Express protection that disclosure does not qualify specific indemnities, completion conditions or agreed price adjustments.

The 22 September 2026 disclosure cut-off also needs updating or confirmation against the current transaction record.

### Buyer knowledge

Reject a bar based on anything “discoverable” from the data room or public records, and blanket imputation of advisers’ knowledge.

Prefer no independent knowledge exclusion. If a compromise is necessary, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals at an agreed date, without constructive knowledge or a duty of inquiry. It must not defeat expressly allocated known-risk indemnities.

Do not allow updated disclosures to cure breaches or shift newly identified risk without Buyer agreement.

## 5. Do not invent consent requirements

- **Office lease:** The supplied material identifies notification, not landlord consent. Verify and comply with the actual notice obligation.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not, by itself, require consent to a share sale. Check the full agreement for a separate change-of-control provision or other trigger.

These should be resolved accurately, rather than converted into unsupported completion conditions.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure clean Completion:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark payoff and release, valid share transfer and Ironquay IP resolution.
2. **Protect the AUD 24m economics:** expressly allocate bonuses/on-costs and correctly classify renewals without double counting.
3. **Restore enforceable remedies:** remove blanket “all Claims” limitations and negotiate distinct protection for fundamental warranties, tax and known risks.
4. **Narrow disclosure and knowledge exclusions:** diligence access must not become acceptance of every discoverable risk.
5. **Resolve the incident uncertainty:** obtain evidence, proportionate contractual protection and, where justified, secured recourse.

The Seller’s statements that matters are “settled”, “adequate” or “not material” are negotiating positions—not conclusions the Buyer should adopt.
